pll2d3c4-d1e3514.summary: Asks whether angels were created good or evil, just or unjust, and whether there was any delay between creation and fall.

pll2d3c4-d1e3517.summary: Reports some who think the fallen angels were created evil, not turning to evil by free choice, with no delay between creation and fall, while the others were created fully blessed. They cite Augustine on Genesis: the devil may have fallen from the beginning, never living blessed; 'he did not stand in the truth' (John 8:44).

pll2d3c4-d1e3550.summary: Further Augustine as cited by them: some think the devil was created in malice, citing Job 40:19 ('the beginning of God's work... to be mocked') and Ps 103:26 ('the dragon you formed to mock him').

pll2d3c4-d1e3584.summary: Adds that they hold the angels who remained were created perfect and blessed, citing Augustine that 'heaven' signifies spiritual creation perfect and blessed from its beginning.

pll2d3c4-d1e3593.summary: Reports another view: all angels were created good, without vice, innocent but not just, lacking virtues, which were given to those who stood when confirmed by grace, while others fell by pride. There was a short interval when all were good by creation; they could sin or not, but could not advance to merit unless grace were added, which was added to some in confirmation.
claims: Angels were created good and innocent but not just.
There was a brief interval before fall or confirmation.
Angels could not merit without added grace.

pll2d3c4-d1e3598.summary: They cite Augustine: angelic nature was first created unformed and called heaven, then formed and called light when converted to the Creator in perfect love ('let there be light').
claims: Angelic nature was formed by conversion to God.

pll2d3c4-d1e3632.summary: Adds that reason opposes the view that angels were created evil: the best Creator cannot be author of evil, so all from him was good; all angels were good when first made, with the goodness of nature just begun.
claims: God cannot author evil.
All angels were created good.

pll2d3c4-d1e3644.summary: Cites Augustine refuting the view: God made all very good, including angelic nature; it is unjust to damn without merit what he created, so the evil will, not nature, is punished. Job 40:19 refers not to the devil's nature but to his aerial body, or God's ordering that makes him useful to the good, or his making: God foresaw his evil will yet made him to benefit the good, so that he is mocked when his temptation profits the saints.
claims: God made angelic nature good.
Evil will, not nature, is punished.
God uses the devil's temptation to benefit the saints.

pll2d3c4-d1e3691.summary: Notes that Augustine thus explains Job and asserts the good creation of angelic nature.
claims: Angelic nature was created good.

pll2d3c4-d1e3697.summary: Cites Augustine on John 8:44: the devil 'never stood in the truth' does not mean he was created evil, since one cannot fall if made evil; made first, he immediately turned from the truth, delighted in his own power, not tasting beatitude, losing it by not willing to receive it; he fell from what he would have received had he willed to submit to God. So there was a very brief interval.
claims: The devil was not created evil.
He fell immediately after creation.
He fell from what he would have received, not from what he had.

pll2d3c4-d1e3709.summary: Cites Origen on Ezekiel: the serpent did not crawl on its belly from the beginning; as Adam and Eve did not sin at once, the serpent was once in paradise not a serpent, since God did not make malice. So he fell after an interval.
claims: God did not make malice.
The devil fell after creation.

pll2d3c4-d1e3735.summary: Interprets John 8:44: 'a murderer from the beginning' means right after the beginning, when he promised himself equality with God and killed himself; 'did not stand in the truth' means he apostatized right after the beginning. Or: from the time man was made, whom he killed by envy and deceived.
claims: 'From the beginning' means immediately after creation.
Alternatively it refers to the devil's murder of man.

pll2d3c4-d1e3771.summary: Concludes that all angels were created good and some fell after creation from the good they would have had had they stood.
claims: All angels were created good.
Some fell after creation.

pl-l2d3c4.summary: Asks whether angels were created good or evil and whether there was any delay between creation and fall. Some held the fallen angels were created evil and fell at once, others created fully blessed, citing Augustine on Genesis ('he did not stand in the truth,' John 8:44; 'the beginning of God's work,' Job 40:19). Others held all were created good, innocent but not yet just (lacking exercised virtues), with a brief interval before fall or confirmation, able to sin or not but unable to merit without added grace; angelic nature was first unformed, then formed by conversion. Reason confirms that the good Creator cannot author evil. Augustine explains Job's text as referring to the devil's aerial body or God's ordering him to benefit the good, and says the devil fell immediately after creation from what he would have received, not from what he had; Origen agrees. So all angels were created good, and some fell after creation.
claims: Some held the fallen angels were created evil.
The better view is that all angels were created good.
Angels were innocent but not yet just, lacking exercised virtues.
There was a brief interval between creation and fall.
The good Creator cannot be the author of evil.
Job 40:19 refers not to the devil's nature but to God's use of him.
The devil fell from the good he would have received, not from what he had.
